Funding decisions would be made by a council of representatives from seven of the 10 University of California campuses — Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco — and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions.
But there are red flags here, as well.
The money is reserved for projects at the institutions represented on the council — raising serious conflict-of-interest concerns. (Proponents said council members would have to abide by ethics and conflict-of-interest regulations — although the measure carves out multiple exceptions — and the council and institute would be subject to independent audits and annual reporting requirements.)
Supporters ask voters to look past these issues by arguing that state-level investment is needed because of President Donald Trump’s funding cuts for medical research. But National Institutes of Health funding for immunotherapy research has steadily risen since 2019 (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/), when it was established as a new category.
Moreover, Robert Kaplan, an opponent of the measure who was an associate director at the National Institutes of Health and formerly led UCLA’s health services program, told us that Prop 38 fundamentally misunderstands how funding top-tier medical research works.
It doesn’t make sense to restrict billions of dollars to just one area of research, Kaplan said. After all, there’s no guarantee that immunology, as opposed to another field of study, holds the cure to cancer or Alzheimer’s. Funding should be prioritized for thoroughly vetted projects that show the greatest promise of making a difference. Limiting the eligibility pool will almost certainly waste money on efforts that lack merit or scientific rigor.
That’s a lesson Californians should be familiar with.
In 2004, voters approved $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research, swayed by the promise of miracle cures and huge financial windfalls for the state. Those didn’t materialize, a Chronicle investigation found (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/?_gl=1*76rb29*_gcl_aw*R0NMLjE3OTAxMTQ1MzUuQ2owS0NRand6c2pWQmhDM0FSSXNBTG5NdjRuS1U2OEx6Z3BLUndsckVzczNmZTNRNXlnVzNYeFI1VUprUDZqcXljR3h5SzFEQzg2QXBDSWFBa1RLRUFMd193Y0I.*_gcl_au*MTYxMzIzNzI3Mi4xNzg4OTExNzQ5*_ga*MTQ1MTQ5NDU3MS4xNzgxMTM0OTQ4*_ga_56G0ZT3ZD0*czE3OTA4MDgxMDkkbzExNCRnMSR0MTc5MDgwODg5MCRqNjAkbDAkaDA.); in fact, the measure may have actually empowered an uptick in clinics peddling pseudoscience.
That didn’t stop voters from approving yet another measure in 2020 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-Prop-14-no-need-to-15592513.php) authorizing $5.5 billion in bonds for stem-cell research.

Let’s not make the same mistake a third time.
There isn’t a family in California who hasn’t been touched by cancer, Alzheimer’s or heart disease. Better treatments and cures cannot come fast enough. We applaud any billionaire who earnestly wants to harness their fortune to fight disease. But if Michelson, Luskin and Milken want Californians to believe that’s their intention with Prop 38, they should spend their own money and come back to taxpayers when their institute actually has some progress to show.

Proposition 38 on the 2026 California ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) will provide vitally needed funding to cure and prevent devastating diseases that impact millions of Californians, including cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's (https://yeson38.com/faq/).
Key reasons to vote YES on Prop 38, the Immunology Medical Research & Cures Initiative:
Helps offset federal cuts to medical research
Prop 38 responds to federal funding cuts and uncertainty (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) that are delaying life-saving medical research.
Dedicated funding for cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease research
Half of all funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) are dedicated specifically to research into cures for Alzheimer's, cancer and heart disease.
Fosters collaboration between leading scientists and physicians
Grants are overseen by an Advisory Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) of leading scientists, doctors and researchers in the field of immunology.
Mandates strong accountability and transparency
State administrative costs are limited to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), with public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Designed to pay for itself – including interest
Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest.
Requires 20% discount on treatments and cures for Californians
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) below the national average.

What does a YES vote on Prop 38 mean?
A YES vote on Prop 38 means California will support $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology research (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at California universities and nonprofit research institutions to find cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and other devastating diseases in our lifetime. Additionally, California patients will get a 20% discount on the cures it helps create (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).

Medical research funded by Prop 38 will be conducted here in California at leading universities and medical research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) that are well-qualified to conduct breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research.

Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.
Why is a voter-backed initiative required rather than a legislative statute?
We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

Myths vs Facts
Get the facts on Prop 38. Learn what the initiative will do and find answers to some of the most common questions about Prop 38.
Updated October 26, 2026
Can California afford Prop 38?
Fact: Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself (https://yeson38.com/get-the-facts/#accountability). 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go back to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), covering both the principal and the interest of the bonds. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most prevalent diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses for Californians by tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses and lower insurance premiums.
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits. Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on saving lives.
For the millions of families that are facing life-threatening and life-altering diseases that take away our loved ones, we can’t afford NOT to invest in promising cures .
Why does California need Prop 38 when the federal government funds medical research too?
Fact: Prop 38 responds to massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty that are shutting down life-saving medical research (https://apnews.com/article/trump-science-medicine-research-cancer-funding-university-0ef3fa47694784e47b0ecd51680410ba) at California universities and research institutes. We are in a race against time, and patients and their loved ones can’t afford to wait.
Prop 38 creates a stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts to accelerate the pace of discoveries to help the tens of millions of patients fighting cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other debilitating diseases.
Prop 38 will make California a national leader in breakthrough medical research , fostering collaboration between leading California-based universities, scientists and physicians.
Prop 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs . Scientific research has become a critical economic engine in California, and studies show (https://www.unitedformedicalresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/UMR_2026-Annual-Economic-Report-FY2025.pdf) that each dollar invested in medical research returns three dollars back into our state’s economy.
Does half of Prop 38 funding go to one research institute?
Fact: Half of Prop 38 funding will support a world-class nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California with access to leading scientists, technology, laboratory equipment, patients and clinical trials necessary to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.
The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy will very likely apply for funding and meet qualification requirements. However, state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific named institute (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-12/) but can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. Ultimately, the California Department of Public Health is charged with determining which institute receives the funds (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm).
Will scientists or politicians decide which research Prop 38 funds?
Fact: Under Prop 38, scientists and researchers oversee a competitive process to ensure the most qualified research with life-saving potential is awarded funding. Prop 38 establishes an Advisory and Accountability Research Council (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), composed of members from seven University of California campuses and 10 – 15 members from California nonprofit universities and academic and research institutions. Each member of the council will be a physician, scientist or researcher with demonstrated experience in the field of immunology and immunotherapy.
Should the private sector fund this research instead of Prop 38?
Fact: Public funding like Prop 38 is vital to support medical research. More than 99% of new FDA-approved drugs from 2010 to 2019 were built on publicly funded research. (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2804378) Prop 38 builds on this proven model by supporting universities and nonprofit researchers to move discoveries from the lab to patients faster and more cost-effectively.
Will the people funding Prop 38 benefit financially?
Fact: Prop 38 is funded by a doctor and philanthropists who will not benefit financially. Only public universities and nonprofit research institutions in California are eligible to receive research funding.
YES on Prop 38 is supported by leading patient advocates (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, Blood Cancer United, American Nurses AssociationCalifornia, Kidney Cancer Association, Melanoma Research Alliance, Parkinson’s Foundation, and Prostate Cancer Foundation, as well as patients, doctors and researchers because it will accelerate life-saving cures. This is a publicly accountable, voter-approved bond.

Retired government analysts raise alarm on immunology bond on November ballot
By Tarini Mehta
September 11, 2026 3:33 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Three former employees of the California Legislative Analyst’s Office came out in strong opposition against Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) Thursday, arguing that the ballot measure that seeks to support medical research lacked appropriate provisions for transparency and accountability. Instead, they said, it seemed to “steer public funds” to its billionaire backer’s “philanthropic project” and then “hide its tracks.”
The proposition (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) will ask voters in the November election to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of medical research grants in recent months. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California appeared (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) to meet the criteria included in the measure for the nonprofit that would be awarded half the bond proceeds. That institute is the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Proposition 38.
‘Hides its tracks’
“Those of you who have worked with the Legislative Analyst’s Office before, you know how reticent our staff is to ever engage in partisan political debates,” said Marianne O’Malley, former managing principal analyst at the LAO, at a virtual news conference organized by the No on Proposition 38 campaign Thursday. “We don’t do that, so you may be wondering why three retired LAO staffers are talking publicly about Proposition 38. The reason is this is no ordinary measure. This measure hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire’s philanthropic project, and then it hides its tracks by waiving all the usual laws to promote governmental transparency.”
O’Malley said it is not uncommon for the government to transfer funds to a nonprofit or private entity to carry out a project. However, such a transfer usually follows an open and competitive bidding process — something Proposition 38 does not seem to do, she said.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign, said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health.
Swanson said the measure was written to allocate funds to an institute that is “ready to go, competitive and world-class.” She said state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific nonprofit, but they can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open soon.
“We don’t have time to wait. Patients don’t have time to wait for another entity to be created,” Swanson said. “We want an institute that’s able to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.”
For O’Malley, the problem with the measure does not end with the selection of the institute. She said Proposition 38 did not have provisions to promote transparency after the money is disbursed. She pointed to a clause that said the chosen nonprofit institute was not to be deemed a public agency. Therefore, it would be immune from public records and open meeting requirements that ordinarily provide accountability over public funds.
Will it pay for itself?
The backers of Proposition 38 argue that it has strong accountability protections, including independent financial audits, annual reports, a citizens’ oversight committee and a 2% cap on state administrative costs, apart from the general transparency rules that all nonprofits must follow.
They also say the measure protects taxpayers and is designed to pay for itself, since 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the total costs of the bond. With the global immunotherapy market projected to grow rapidly over the next decade, supporters believe the research program created under Proposition 38 will create “more than enough revenue.” In addition, treatments developed through funded research are to be offered at a 20% discount in California.
However, Dan Carson, also a former LAO analyst, disputed that claim based on California’s experience with stem-cell research bonds passed in 2004 and 2020. In 2004, voters approved Proposition 71, creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine and authorizing $3 billion in bond funding for stem cell research. Californians approved an additional $5.5 billion for the institute in 2020.
During his time at the LAO, Carson said he worked on a team that analyzed Proposition 71 and found that it had failed to deliver on the huge financial windfall it had promised the state.
“The state eventually received only a tiny fraction of the billions of dollars we were promised,” he said. “We got about $16 million in payoff for intellectual property, and we were projected to spend about $6 billion over time to repay the principal and interest on those bonds. So here we go again with Prop. 38. This time, an even bigger $8.4 billion medical research bond issue that will cost us roughly half a billion dollars a year for decades to pay off.”
The research topics eligible for funding under the bond measure include understanding disease formation and factors that contribute to the same. While those research activities are important, Carson said, they do not directly develop new cures that can generate assets to pay off the bond costs. However, the measure does ask that projects with the “greatest potential for yielding the most immediate, accessible and affordable therapies” be prioritized in the competitive research grant selections.

‘Institutional favoritism’
Those selections, for the half of the money that will not go to the single institute, will be made by a council consisting of representatives of the University of California campuses, nonprofit universities and research institutions in consultation with the selected institute. The grants will be awarded to universities and institutions represented on the council.
According to Judy Heiman, former principal analyst at the LAO, that creates a conflict of interest which will result in members of a closed group discussing how to divide up $4.2 billion amongst themselves rather than finding the best uses for the money.
“There’s a legitimate argument about whether California should add billions of dollars in medical research spending to its already substantial debt burden,” Heiman said. “Those who think we shouldn’t will vote against Prop. 38. I would argue that even those who would like to see a major state investment in research should vote no on Prop. 38 and demand an open, transparent and accountable structure. Scientific merit, not institutional favoritism, should drive where the money goes.”
The No on Proposition 38 campaign, led by Stanford Universitysenior scholar Robert Kaplan (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html), has so far not reported any contributions. Kaplan has consistently criticized the practice of funding research focused on specific diseases rather than investing in medical research more broadly, especially when the Trump administration’s cuts affected public health programs across the board.
Support for Prop. 38
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $27 million so far, of which more than $22 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy.
The measure has the endorsement of the California Democratic Party and the California Republican Party. It is also supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association.
Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor whose life was saved by an immunotherapy clinical trial at UCLA, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California, but the country and the whole world.
“I lived through struggling to find new treatments for 12 years. I had heard about CAR T-cell therapy in 2012, but I had to wait six years for it to make it into trial because these things are not enough of a priority,” Adami said. “Everybody says the federal government will restore (research funding). I’m sorry, patients can’t wait for that, just like I couldn’t. If my trial hadn’t opened, I was a month away from dying. That’s how sick I was, and this is the case for too many people.”
In November, Prop. 38 will need “yes” votes from a majority of California voters to be approved.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

Background
Founded by visionary philanthropists Dr. Gary Michelson, Dr. Eric Esrailian, Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken and Sean Parker, the CIII was formally established as a public-private partnership with the State of California. (Governor Newsom Announces World-Leading Science & Technology Research Center in Los Angeles (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/)). The CIII will be operated as an independent medical research organization, with faculty affiliated with the renowned David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA.
Also home to UCLA Center for Quantum Science and Engineering (https://www.cqse.ucla.edu/index.html), UCLA Research Park will be the world’s first facility to bring together immunology, quantum computing, and AI, together with translational research and product development capacity, biotech incubator and accelerator space. As an economic engine for Southern California, CIII will rapidly become the world's epicenter for innovation for immunologically-based health solutions.
Next Steps
Building on its momentum, CIII is:
Developing its initial five year strategic plan (2025-2029)
Recruiting senior scientific and executive leadership
Identifying and securing philanthropic and industrial partners
Planning, designing and building the research facilities at UCLA Research Park
Establishing its governing board, scientific, and other advisory committees
By creating a unique culture of convergent biological and computer sciences entrepreneurial research and industrial partnerships, laser focused on harnessing the power of the human immune system, the CIII offers the potential to rapidly discover and develop new technologies and products to prevent, treat and cure humanity’s most intractable diseases.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.
Why is a voter-backed initiative required rather than a legislative statute?
We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.
